title: The Pietists
hookLine: Spener and the Pietists gather small groups to read the Bible and live it warmly

lines: A FEW CHAIRS AND A BIBLE.
cards: What happens to a sermon after the last hymn? People shake hands at the door, go home, eat lunch. By Tuesday, it's mostly gone.

A Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt named Philipp Jakob Spener worried about exactly that. His church had careful teaching, strong doctrine, faithful services. And yet faith, to him, seemed to stop at the church door.
So he tried something small. He invited a few people to his house during the week to talk over the sermon and read the Bible together. Not a new church.
Just a few chairs, an open book, and a question: how do we actually live this?

teach.b: Spener wrote his hopes for the church in a short book called Pia Desideria, a Latin title usually rendered as pious longings, or heartfelt desires.
Among them: that ordinary Christians would read the whole Bible, not just hear bits of it on Sunday.

That every believer would take part in the church's life, not only the clergy, an echo of Luther's priesthood of all believers. That faith would show up in love, in how people actually treated each other.
And that arguments about doctrine would be carried on with charity, not cruelty. The small groups that met in his home and others like them were sometimes called gatherings of piety.
Critics called them Pietists, and in time the movement carried the name. Spener wasn't trying to throw out Lutheran teaching. He was trying to warm it.

The Pietists spoke of a heart religion: faith you don't just agree to, but live. They found a model in the letter of James, in the King James words: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only."
And Jesus' promise in Matthew sets the size: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."
The movement had its tensions; some church leaders worried small groups would split congregations, and the Pietists argued about that among themselves. But the idea traveled.
A Bible study or house group today can look a lot like Spener's living room.

how: Christians in different churches meet in small groups, often in homes, to read a passage of the Bible together, talk about how to live it, and pray for one another.

o: Lutherans who met in small groups to read and live the Bible
scholars who argued doctrine at the great universities
Catholics who left the church to pray alone in the woods

p: faith you live, not just agree to

s: Spener set out to start a new church
he wanted to warm Lutheran faith from inside, not throw out its teaching.
Spener hoped ordinary Christians would read the whole Bible
it was one of the hopes in Pia Desideria, along with every believer taking part.
'Pietist' began as a name the movement chose for itself
it was a name critics used, and in time the movement carried it.

games.q: you're a pastor. your services are faithful, but faith seems to stop at the church door. what do you try?
o: invite a few people home midweek to read the Bible together.
games.why: Spener gathered small groups in his home to talk over the sermon and read scripture, and the idea spread.

practice: Bring to mind two or three people you could sit with, at a kitchen table or on a video call, to read something that matters and talk about living it. Hold their faces in the quiet.
If you pray, pray for them by name or rest with where two or three are gathered; if you don't, simply hold the picture of that table.

wordCard.voice: The Pietists. A movement inside Lutheran churches, sparked by Spener, that gathered small groups to read the Bible together and live their faith warmly.

orig.note: Latin, the title of Spener's book: pious longings, heartfelt desires.

carryVoice: Your line: a heart religion. Faith that walks out the church door with you. See you tomorrow.
